title: This Is a Serious Mistake
description:
Ben Shapiro went on Gavin Newsom’s podcast and argued that institutional investors are helping housing because rents are down.

Rents dipping doesn’t help first-time buyers when home prices have doubled, institutional ownership is exploding, and Americans are being priced out of owning anything at all.

We break down the numbers Ben blurred, the rent vs. ownership sleight of hand, and why “just rent forever” isn’t a solution, it’s a trap.

comments.text:
I owned , a major construction company, was sold to private equity in 2023. Private equity is hollowing out the country. It is not limited to institutional investors buying single-family homes. They are quietly absorbing local electrical, plumbing, and trade businesses, preserving the appearance of small, independent operators while ownership is centralized under financial institutions. Most people miss this because it looks local on the surface. It is not just housing being consolidated; it is the productive economy itself.

I sold my own company for millions, yet after the sale the entire operation was restructured in a way that abandoned the philosophy it was built on. That is the standard private-equity playbook.

There is another hard reality people avoid that if illegal labor is removed from the construction pipeline, housing and build costs will spike easily triple, and in some cases quadruple for repairs and specialty work. Insurance costs will follow. New construction will become astronomically expensive, and those costs will be passed directly to American consumers.

There is no clean solution. Sometimes there is no correct answer, only tradeoffs. But Ben’s implication is wrong, and Steven’s implications are also wrong. Both analyses ignore the structural consequences already locked into the system.

The free market works for those at the bottom if you are at a place where it appears as if infinite growth was possible.

When a resource is limited, like space where you’re allowed to to build sheet at a location where you want the sheet to be (could be cities, could be some place with infrastructure), the free market doesn‘t work for those at the bottom. You then have a shortage of supply that can‘t be filled by free actors that don‘t already own lots of sheet, and then you‘re moving towards something I’d describe as a supplier-oligopoly-like environment.

So there‘s no free market. So you need the governent, at least to some extent. I love the free market so it‘s painful to say that when it comes to housing, there‘s a limit to how much inequality you can tolerate if you want to uphold an upwards trajectory for the lower and lower middle class to be readily available.

And yes, if you have fewer migrants, there‘ll be less demand for housing, so that‘s good. More power to the remaining demanders 😉
